doc.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999

chapter: Finding her voice as a composer
title: Japanese heritage in jazz; Duke Ellington's death and the years of playing
summary: Being Japanese was seen as a handicap; Duke Ellington's death and a Hentoff memoir led her to explore her heritage, drawing on her years sitting in with greats.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: No. Actually I never thought about it until Duke Ellington died. Before that, you know it was just a Japanese traditional concept, or being Japanese playing jazz was some sort of a handicap. When I was growing up in Japan as a player, they always said that Filipino people have better feeling than Japanese, and indeed the Filipino players played better than us, and it’s simply because they have a longer history. They weren’t under — they were colonized by America so they are more exposed for jazz, much longer than we were. I think that would have to be. Today no one say that anymore. So when I was in Japan a critical compliment to me, and the phrases they used was, “Her playing smells of

butter.” The smell of butter means very American. Because butter is western. Japanese traditionally, we have no butter. So they used to say her playing smells of butter. That’s what they used to say. So that has been going on for a long time. When Duke Ellington died, it was ’73, or ’74 I think, and there was a Village Voice, Nat Hentoff had a memoir. And he was talking about that fact that Duke was, how proud he was about his race. And he was pointing out so many music was based on his race, which I knew some but I never thought of it that way until someone pointed — “Black Butterfly” “Black and Tan Fantasy,” what have you. So that’s what actually triggered me. I think everything you do is sort of inviting. The dark time comes because everything else is something developing underneath. And it’s almost like a volcano and if something triggers it that becomes. I think in my case it was Duke Ellington, that memoir, written by Nat Hentoff. And I thought that’s what I should — I should look into my heritage before, because one I have a long career as a jazz player and I came a very good time in this country where no one cares and no club owner would cares if you pack them in or not. You will do the routine, the circuit, the jazz club circuit. Even for example the greatest classic Miles Davis Quintet, like Red Garland, Philly Jo, Coltrane, Paul Chambers. The people did not come. I mean at Storyville they’d come only, the weekend was the only time. On the weeknights, not that many people were there. Those are the times. But the clubs wasn’t so uptight about that. So I caught the tail end of that I went through. Also the great players like Oscar Pettiford was living and he used to come to the Hickory House when I was playing in the summertime, almost every night, sitting in, meaning he didn’t have a job. You know in those days, I feel very bad for him but at the same time those were the days that if people didn’t have a job, and they were great players, and the jazz music business wasn’t quite so organized or productionized as of today. They were very open, so I could sit in with Monk’s group if I know the tune, which I did, and things like that. That was my very valuable asset. And all that I think was the basic foundation of my writing. So my long years of playing and the timing was right for me to come to this country, to be able to play with these players was the most valuable lesson you could possibly get. I think that is my asset, not everybody can have. So I sort of wait, where I’ve had a long career as a jazz player, but I have a different heritage, and always I never even thought about looking into my heritage. But because of the article I said I would look into it. Probably I have a different heritage than American players, and I should try to draw from that, perhaps I can make it a little bit different. As you know jazz history and music history did not include the oriental influence. So at least I can infuse something to make it a little bit different and perhaps I can return something to the jazz
